newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl heads for Latin America to boost trade.
newsitem.headline: Kohl heads for Latin America to boost trade.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl heads for Latin America next week hoping to boost trade with three countries which traditionally have strong ties with Germany, and encourage a continuation of economic reform programmes.
His eight-day tour starting on Sunday takes him to Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, three of Latin America's most important economies and among the leading locations for German investment abroad.

Despite the attention attracted by fast-growing economies in southeast Asia, these have drawn only 16.4 billion marks ($10.84 billion) of German direct investment compared with a cumulative 21.2 billion in Latin America as a whole.

With Latin American economies bringing inflation under control and providing political stability, German companies are keen to capitalise on steady growth rates and on a number of large-scale privatisation programmes, government officials say.
"In the last five or 10 years Latin America has made enormous strides and it's now very much 'in' again," said one government official.

Representatives from 17 major companies including car and aerospace concern Daimler-Benz, carmaker Volkswagen, electronics giant Siemens and chemicals firm Degussa will accompany Kohl or join his discussions.
The volume of trade between Germany and the three countries was valued at almost 21 billion marks in 1995.

Such is the flow of business that officials see no need to use the visit to accelerate the signing of a clutch of commercial contracts. They say business is brisk enough not to need such an added helping hand.

To underline the importance of German investment, Kohl will see two German automobile models start to roll off production lines: Mercedes-Benz's Sprinter van at a plant near Buenos Aires and Volkswagen's new Beetle at its Puebla plant in Mexico.

Hans Peter Stihl, chairman of German industry's Latin America initiative founded last year, told the daily Handelsblatt he hoped Kohl's visit would accelerate attempts to sign an investor protection agreement with Mexico.
Mexico is also likely to lobby Kohl to help secure institutional economic links with the European Union which go beyond the step-by-step liberalisation of trade now on offer.

Mexico, which does most of its trade with the neighbouring United States and is a member of the North Atlantic Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), is keen to have a free trade agreement with the EU as a second pillar of its foreign commerce, Bonn officials say.

Kohl is likely to express his appreciation in all three countries for recent economic advances which have presented opportunities for German firms, such as privatisation in Argentina's telecommunications sector.
But he will also urge more liberalisation, for instance by encouraging Brazil to ease or remove limits on vehicle and wine imports.
While Kohl last visited Argentina and Mexico in 1984 and 1986 respectively, he travelled to Brazil as recently as 1991, and again in 1992 for the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

Bonn officials say the fact that he has chosen to visit Brazil again, albeit only for just over 24 hours, is a conscious gesture of recognition for Brazil's growing political weight in world affairs. ($1=1.5134 Mark)
